Anthropic’s Towards Monosemanticity[10]Towards Monosemanticity: Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary LearningBricken, T., Templeton, A., Batson, J., et al., 2023. Transformer Circuits Thread. References ↓ (2023), studying a small one-layer model, gave the median neuron a 0 on its rubric out of a possible 14, meaning the rater couldn’t form any hypothesis. The automated interpretability project[8]Language Models Can Explain Neurons in Language ModelsBills, S., Cammarata, N., Mossing, D., et al., 2023. OpenAI. References ↓ I started at OpenAI (also 2023) found about 1.7% of neurons interpretable by our most generous measure.

With better tools and modern models, the situation looks quite different. In preliminary audits of Qwen3-32B, we estimate that roughly 90% of neuron poles have one main job, often with small related offshoots; another ~7% have two related jobs; and only ~2-4% are not yet understood1A note on this number: the share of neurons with one job varies depending on how you set the threshold for counting weak activations, depth, density of sub-circuits, and what you view as “one thing”.How far to go into weak activations is a big factor here. There’s a section describing weak activations below. It tends to increase how many “related things” there are, more than whether the neuron is a judgement of something legible. For instance, the Trump neuron’s weak activations bring in MAGA hats and people related to him. The Titanic neuron’s weak activations bring in stories of more general voyages, or steam engines and other technologies of the era.There’s also the question of whether to care about activation percentiles, or fraction of the strongest activations. In general I think what the neuron learns should be trusted, its natural sparsity and activation ranges and so on. Which I used to mostly not believe! I’m somewhat against trying to standardize things across all neurons. Percentiles are more common today, I think because they’re easier to think about.It goes the other way too. For instance, when you look at the Titanic neuron’s “unrelated jobs,” it’s often detecting that “boat” comes next. The tool missed this because it only looked backward when judging context. When we look at these “unrelated jobs” in depth, it’s almost always this kind of thing. It’s easy to build an imperfect tool.Overall, I don’t think coming to a single score is actually that important. But when it was taken out, early reviewers felt unanchored without even a rough number. In the sets I’ve looked at more closely, considering strong activations, it’s closer to 97% non-arbitrary mixtures, but these are relatively small samples.Overall distilling everything into one “cleanliness” score should be taken as a broad pointer to the regime a neural network is in, rather than something precise to either optimize directly or hold too tightly. A lot of this essay is for being less dimensionality reduced, treating each neuron and circuit differently, according to their motifs, depth, role etc. Despite this, a rough number can be useful.. Dense and Mixture of Experts models seem roughly similar. We found similar results in models up to trillions of parameters, like Kimi K3, which the companion paper will cover in more detail. These percentages compress a high-dimensional picture into a few numbers, and the precise number depends on where you set thresholds for what counts as “one thing” – like whether you lump together closely related idioms in two languages. I don’t think much in interpretability hangs on that question. What matters a lot more is why things share a neuron in the first place.

Most of the remaining apparent polysemanticity seems to be a motif I call recursive generalization. It’s simple: as a neuron grows, it sprouts offshoots the way a tree branch sprouts sub-branches. For instance, one neuron that detected “iy” grew to detect “diy,” and then “do it yourself,” which doesn’t contain “iy” at all. This idea first appeared in a forgotten subsection of a paper I worked on called Multimodal Neurons[3]Multimodal Neurons in Artificial Neural NetworksGoh, G., Cammarata, N., Voss, C., et al., 2021. Distill. References ↓ (2021). At the time, I hadn’t watched neurons grow over training. Now it’s easier, and it holds up everywhere I’ve seen. Even the original InceptionV1 wasn’t knotted. When I retrain its original architecture, which still produces messy deep layers, and follow the least legible neurons I can find, they turn out to be overgrowing locally into reasonable, adjacent territory.

So there were two explanations for polysemanticity, and I helped propose both. In some ways, they’re opposites: generalization groups similar things together and superposition groups unrelated things together. Superposition is the one the field bet on and, until recently, so did I. But I now think recursive generalization was basically right. That leaves one learning principle after all. It’s still generalization, but it turns out generalization is fractal. That’s far less concerning: there’s something to learn from the way things were grouped, and nothing to learn from two items in superposition. And since the generalization itself is fractal, our explanations can be too: start with a basic explanation, then zoom in when you want to understand more. In that sense, almost the entire network is interpretable if we look closely enough, especially if we look at how it grew over training.

Why was the gap so large? I think several ordinary problems compounded. The explainer models of 2023 couldn’t run the loop of conjecture and test; the tools and metrics were weak, rewarding explanations that could simulate activations rather than ones that were right, which often come apart; no one knew what language neuron motifs to expect, and people broadly looked for the wrong kinds of things; and most studies used small or simplified models. In a sense, those models really had run out of room, which made superposition the natural explanation. But a network short on room doesn’t switch learning principles; its neurons just get broader, as in the small vision models. Broad neurons are usually easy to break down once you know what to look for. Without that knowledge, and with primitive tools, they look like arbitrary mixtures.

Interpretability has a surprising amount of momentum: like a jigsaw puzzle or crossword, any understanding you gain starts constraining the rest of the system. At first, you’re looking at a single neuron. If you can’t understand it, little else helps: circuits and attribution graphs only explain a neuron in terms of other neurons you don’t understand yet. This can make getting started hard. Once the map starts to fill in, though, it goes surprisingly well. If you don’t understand exactly what a neuron does, you can study what it connects to, the ecosystem around it, and – in a mixture-of-experts model – what its expert specializes in. As with a puzzle coming together, every piece comes with many clues, and they’re well structured and easy to run experiments against. That’s why nearly empty and mostly filled in aren’t surprising places to be; they’re the natural anchors.

Take a neuron that tracks ‘a sense of righteousness when a bargain purchase turns out to work better than the expensive alternative’. Neurons that track a feeling or social cue like this are some of the most common we’ve found. Imagine finding this one with no knowledge of language neuron motifs and no circuits to lean on, because few neighboring neurons are explained yet. Most humans and agents expect neurons to detect nouns by firing on them, which they mostly don’t. Look at where this one fires most strongly, and you see a pile of seemingly unrelated commas.

Now imagine the map is mostly filled in. You know many neurons detect subtle feelings or social contexts, and that they often fire not on the words that carry the feeling but on punctuation, like commas, where the model summarizes what a sentence meant, or on the word just before the feeling matters for predicting what comes next. So you read the surrounding sentences instead, and check its steering effects (what the model writes when you turn the neuron up), which line up closely. You look upstream at how it’s built and downstream at what it does, and both line up. You check its negative pole, what pushes it strongly negative, and find a subtle variant of the same cue, or the moment the social context ends. You can run specific tests, like checking which store brands it responds to. Any of these could break the explanation, yet they keep pointing to the same place. And understanding this neuron sharpens the broader motif: after thousands of subtle-feeling and social-context detectors, you start to know what to expect from the next one, which is part of why the map fills in faster as it goes.

It works on the tools too. When you can see 2% of a network, you can’t tell where your tools are broken; when you can see most of it, the unexplained remainder points straight at them. That’s how some coworkers and I found a double-negative regime in SwiGLU neurons that, as far as we know, no one had noticed, and that a decomposition mixing many neurons together would likely have hidden.

The bad news about modern neural networks is that they're enormous. The good news is that the enormity helps: as the map fills in, every explanation is tightly constrained by everything around it, and bigger models learn narrower neurons that are easier to recognize in the first place.

In this sense, understanding the whole network may be easier than understanding just the parts we care about most. First, it’s hard to know how to think like a neural network until you’ve studied it closely. For instance, “deception” is a useful initial frame, but the building blocks that contribute to deceptive behavior by models probably have alignment-relevant microstructure that will be hard to know without going in and looking. Second, targeting a small set of mechanisms is like working on one row of an otherwise empty crossword. It’s doable, and might work, but without the crossings it’s hard to know whether you’re right. It may be easier to solve the whole thing – or at least the broader parts of the network these mechanisms connect to.

When I ran this process on modern convolutional networks, it basically worked. Agents can map out neurons and circuits, build explorable microscopes and explore them, test explanations thoroughly, and track hundreds of thousands of attribution graphs. There was never a point where rapid normal science broke down. I now feel I basically understand these models, at least enough to know where I’d start asking any question I had; eventually, the crossword just got filled in. So far it has worked in language models too, up to trillions of parameters. Those aren’t close to solved due to sheer size, but I’m optimistic about scaling the process.

All of this has brought me back to an old hope: understanding a neural network directly, by studying its mechanisms and the data flowing between them, without first trying to fix or untangle it. Put together, the argument has four steps.

That’s been the pattern for deep learning in general: the simple thing at absurd scale beats the clever one. Rich Sutton called it the bitter lesson[22]The Bitter LessonSutton, R., 2019. Incomplete Ideas. References ↓. Maybe there’s a bitter lesson for interpretability too: scaling ordinary investigation beats engineering a clever new decomposition.

A technical companion paper will offer a more detailed account of language model neuron experiments, such as what we’ve found about the different regimes of modern non-linearities and what kinds of circuit motifs show up at different depths. This essay glances at many places and conjectures about where it all might be pointing.

The most famous polysemantic neuron is 4e:55 of InceptionV1, which looked like an arbitrary mixture of cats and cars. It’s been brought up as evidence that neurons might not be the right unit of study in several of the field’s most widely read papers, from Feature Visualization[1]Feature VisualizationOlah, C., Mordvintsev, A. and Schubert, L., 2017. Distill. References ↓ in 2017 to Zoom In[4]Zoom In: An Introduction to CircuitsOlah, C., Cammarata, N., Schubert, L., Goh, G., Petrov, M. and Carter, S., 2020. Distill. References ↓. In Zoom In, which I co-authored, we said outright that it “isn’t responding to some commonality of cars and cat faces”.2In Multimodal Neurons we came very close. We asked whether the neuron might be responding to some shared feature, “perhaps cat eyes and car lights look similar,” then decided from the feature visualization’s whiskers and chrome that it was “genuinely OR(cat, car).” We were right to look for a shared shape, but I think we underestimated how far generalization reaches. The shared feature was the V. I think the whiskers misled us because generalization happens inside high-level patterns. The V neuron really does take in cat circuitry, and feature visualization’s job is to raise the activation, so once it finds the cat route it adds everything that route brings. The whiskers come along for the ride, even if the neuron doesn’t “want” them. Downstream, the car readers do get a little cat signal through the V neuron, but it barely reaches the output: one cat detector firing does little on its own, since many work together, so the network never needs a negative weight to cancel it. To see the shared pattern, you have to visualize what the neuron’s inputs have in common, not the neuron on its own.

After months of seeing clean neurons, I wondered if we’d misinterpreted some early prominent examples of polysemanticity and superposition. The canonical polysemantic neuron seemed like the obvious place to check, so I opened up the cat and car image grid I’d seen hundreds of times before and did something I’d never done: I spent a few seconds wondering what one thing this might be. Almost instantly it was obvious: it’s not a cat and car neuron, it’s a V-shape neuron.

I looked at its circuit connections: V-shaped flames, V-shaped water jets from a fireboat, V-shaped fox faces. I looked at its negative pole: an O, round where the V is pointed. Why would an arbitrary mixture of cats and cars need to connect so strongly to a flame?

Then I went to the canonical superposition circuit I first found in 20193I found it while building my first Circuits interface, which only had feature visualization and weights connecting their neurons. Then I took them to Chris Olah and asked why the car would be going into these dogs like this. We came to the conclusion it must be doing a kind of folding, and called it superposition. It was an intuitive explanation for what we saw, so it didn’t prompt diving more into the tools, which would have revealed feature visualization reward hacking and various other things. It being placed into a high-dimensional space felt like a reasonable answer.. The V neuron and this circuit were Zoom In[4]Zoom In: An Introduction to CircuitsOlah, C., Cammarata, N., Schubert, L., Goh, G., Petrov, M. and Carter, S., 2020. Distill. References ↓’s two main examples of why its picture of neurons, that nearly every one turns out to be understandable if you look seriously, might be “overly rosy”.

The circuit appeared to show a car going into a bunch of unrelated dogs, as if the dogs were a kind of high-dimensional storage place where the car could be recovered later as needed.

But that’s not what the car was doing. Cars and dogs were being brought together because of shared pose. InceptionV1 has more than a hundred of these generalized pose neurons, each one its own clean detector of a pose shared across cars, dogs and other objects, and to my knowledge no one had noticed them. Later layers keep building on them, all the way to the end of the model. The car was not being stored in an obscure place, and nothing directly reads out the combination. It’s the opposite: it’s continuing to differentiate into car specialists and finer poses.

Part of the reason was not knowing about generalized pose neurons, and part of the reason is that the technique we use to render icons of images — feature visualization — ends up being reward hacked in deeper layers. The intent is to find an image that maximizes the neuron, but the way that’s done is through gradient descent, and it takes the easiest path, which in InceptionV1 often means dogs. There are lots of dogs in InceptionV1’s training data and a lot of dog neurons, and the early optimization falls into them and never recovers. If you even lightly bias it toward the natural paths the top images take, most of them are cars, and some are both dogs and cars, because of shared pose.

news.title: Perplexity open sources SPACE, its AI agent sandbox, and says partners including CoreWeave, Akamai, and Crusoe agreed to offer SPACE to customers (Reed Albergotti/Semafor)
news.title_en: Perplexity open sources SPACE, its AI agent sandbox, and says partners including CoreWeave, Akamai, and Crusoe agreed to offer SPACE to customers (Reed Albergotti/Semafor)
news.author: Semafor
news.article_content:
Perplexity is giving away the software it has been using to combat rogue AI agents, the company told Semafor Thursday.

Its “AI sandbox,” which it calls SPACE, is now an open source project, allowing outside developers to use the tool, which it says can keep AI agents contained. Perplexity said it’s lined up partners, including CoreWeave, Akamai and Crusoe, which have agreed to offer SPACE to customers.

Sandboxes, or isolated environments for testing and running AI models, have become a hot topic in the tech industry in the wake of reports from AI labs of models escaping their constraints, finding their way onto the open web and hacking unsuspecting victims like Hugging Face and the Australian government.

While AI companies focus on “alignment,” or training models to behave themselves, the security industry has been increasingly advocating erecting strict guardrails around AI models.

“A lot of companies are thinking about how to build secure AI agents, and in many cases they hit a wall,” said Zibi Braniecki, a member of the technical staff at Perplexity, in an interview with Semafor. “We have a solution.”

Perplexity said it tested SPACE by giving nine frontier models instructions to try to break out. In 118 tries, none of them did, while Perplexity found they were able to break out of other sandboxes that were not open sourced.

Braniecki likened the effort to make SPACE open source to what happened with web browsers as the internet developed — companies came together to build guardrails that allowed secure browsing and online commerce. “Right now, we’re thinking too small,” he said.

Other companies like Nvidia have also released open-source security tools, such as Nvidia OpenShell, which runs AI agents in a sandbox and limits what they can reach.

Perplexity said SPACE also helps reduce wasted compute, which can be a byproduct of strict sandboxing.

news.title: Sources: top DOJ officials halt career prosecutors' Biden-era investigation of Meta over facilitating illegal drug sales and are weighing more lenient options (Ben Penn/Bloomberg Law)

news.author: Bloomberg Law
news.article_content:

Top Justice Department officials have sidelined career prosecutors’ long-running grand jury investigation of Meta Platforms over facilitating illegal pharmaceutical sales, just after company executives were subpoenaed to testify, two people familiar with the matter said.

Senior leaders at DOJ headquarters ordered career prosecutors in the Western District of Virginia to cease the criminal investigation following advocacy from Meta‘s legal team, the individuals said. The Trump-appointed officials are contemplating a path to quickly resolve the sprawling opioids case stemming from the Biden administration, they said, adding that Meta executives are no longer being summoned to the grand jury.

The officials — including acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter and his No. 2 Aakash Singh — are considering a civil resolution with a fine or a non-prosecution agreement, added one of the people. Such a deal would allow the social media giant to avoid charges for its role in creating a market for youth to purchase deadly fentanyl pills and other addictive drugs.

Department leaders intervened to protect the company as its founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg has played a core role shaping President Donald Trump’s strategy to counter growing backlash over the safety of AI technology. While the Trump administration has retreated on a wide range of other corporate investigations inherited from the Biden era, this probe was initially allowed to continue when Meta lawyers elevated it to political leadership of DOJ last year, said two people, who like others spoke anonymously about an ongoing case.

Officials are now mulling a range of more lenient options that fall short of the drug trafficking theory pursued by the Appalachia-based Western Virginia district known for aggressive corporate pharmaceutical prosecutions holding chief executives accountable, the individuals said.

The investigation arose during the Covid-19 pandemic when Meta and other social media behemoths faced public and congressional scrutiny for allowing the promotion of prescription drugs to children on their platforms, and for potentially profiting off of users’ illicit transactions. Political and career supervisors overseeing the case have at various points debated its strength, given the challenge of proving criminal intent of far removed Meta executives, said two people briefed on the situation.

Meta assembled a team of prominent defense lawyers from Davis Polk & Wardwell, former Republican Deputy AG Mark Filip of Kirkland & Ellis, and Sullivan & Cromwell — which represents Trump personally in criminal and civil litigation — throughout the history of this case, several people said.

The more recent subpoenas to executives prompted Meta to escalate its concerns to the top of DOJ, leading officials to convene the latest meeting between Filip, Davis Polk lawyers, Meta’s in-house counsel, and the Western District of Virginia prosecutors. Career prosecutors were then told to retreat from their grand jury investigation, the individuals added.

It’s not clear whether prosecutors were targeting particular executives for individual charges or if they were seen as witnesses in a corporate prosecution.

Defense lawyers pointed to instances in which Meta has cooperated with law enforcement by flagging possible illicit drug promotions on its site and has taken steps to mitigate future risks, said one of the individuals. The company also announced partnerships with law enforcement in September for an “anti-scam education campaign” to support Asia-Pacific markets and issued a threat report in March highlighting its increased efforts to combat cartels and other drug-related gang activity.

The existence of this DOJ investigation of Meta was first reported in the Wall Street Journal in 2024.

A spokesperson for the US attorney’s office in Western Virginia deferred comment to DOJ headquarters.

“The Department of Justice cannot comment on ongoing investigations or negotiations. However, this Department has ended the Biden-era days of aggressively and indiscriminately targeting corporations and businesses,” department spokesperson Kiersten Pels said in a statement. “Instead, we are focused on following the facts and the law to surgically address corporate wrongdoing.”

The Trump DOJ has recently overruled career prosecutors seeking criminal charges against other global corporations facing investigations for consumer health and safety.

That includes a criminal case against Abbott Laboratories stemming from contaminated baby formula that resulted in a $385 million civil settlement, and a non-prosecution agreement with Chinese tech company Alibaba Group Holding Ltd, which agreed to pay $600 million over accusations it failed to prevent illegal pharmaceutical sales. CBS News reported earlier on DOJ’s internal dispute over the Alibaba case.

Meta’s probe was led by Randy Ramseyer, the veteran Abingdon, Va.-based assistant US attorney who has long chased Big Pharma heavyweights from Purdue to Abbott on theories of misbranding opioids. Ramseyer is held in high regard by colleagues and feared in the defense bar for his hardball tactics. Pharma companies in prior administrations have also lobbied Main Justice for relief from Ramseyer.

He pulled off the rare feat of putting a pharmaceutical CEO in prison late in Trump’s first term. Lately, however, Ramseyer and his district appear to be losing clout to defendants and Main justice. Under the leadership of Western Virginia’s top prosecutor Robert Tracci, whom the administration installed after it pushed out Trump’s first selection for the post last year, the office also experienced a Washington intervention to scuttle another of its multi-year opioids investigations over the summer.

Swedish pharmaceutical company Orexo announced in August that it had reached a non-binding settlement with the department to end the probe, which two people familiar with the matter said resulted from defense lawyers elevating the case to DOJ leadership.

news.title: Volvo says it will use Nvidia's Hyperion platform to launch a Level 2++ hands-free, point-to-point automated driving system by 2030 (Andrew J. Hawkins/The Verge)
news.title_en: Volvo says it will use Nvidia's Hyperion platform to launch a Level 2++ hands-free, point-to-point automated driving system by 2030 (Andrew J. Hawkins/The Verge)
news.author: The Verge
news.article_content:

The system will be similar to Tesla’s Full Self-Driving in that it will enable hands-free, point-to-point partially automated driving on local roads.

Andrew J. HawkinsCloseAndrew J. HawkinsTransportation editorPosts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

ShareGiftImage: VolvoAndrew J. HawkinsCloseAndrew J. HawkinsPosts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Volvo plans to launch hands-free, point-to-point driving by 2030, powered by Nvidia’s latest AI technology. The Chinese-owned, Swedish-designed automaker said Thursday it would use Nvidia’s autonomous driving stack to power a new partially automated driving system similar to Tesla’s Full Self-Driving (Supervised).

Volvo says the new point-to-point system will be Level 2++, meaning it can handle complex urban environments, including traffic lights, stop signs, and unprotected left turns without explicit driver control. In addition to Tesla’s FSD, it will also resemble the Nvidia-powered system that Mercedes-Benz recently rolled out for the all-new CLA sedan, said Ali Kani, VP and general manager of the automotive team at Nvidia, in an interview with The Verge.

Volvo will use Nvidia’s Hyperion platform, which includes the chipmaker’s high-powered silicon, as well as additional sensors mounted around the vehicle so the car can see and perceive its surroundings. The automaker will also utilize Nvidia’s Alpamayo software, which uses “reasoning” models to make sense of complex road conditions and plan where to steer, brake, or accelerate. The setup will not include lidar, though it could include the laser sensor if Volvo decides to add it in the future.

By expanding its preexisting partnership with Volvo, the automaker is trying to correct some of its failed automated driving projects of the past. The automaker had to effectively sideline its Ride Pilot Level 3 unsupervised autonomous driving system in the US after failing to obtain regulatory approval. Volvo also planned to add lidar sensors to some of its models, but that plan fell away after its supplier Luminar went bankrupt.

Volvo is also bringing its own reputation for safety to the table. The automaker wants to combine its safety expertise with Nvidia’s technology to improve the overall system, including contributing its proprietary driver-understanding systems, which analyze driver behavior in considerably greater detail than a basic driver monitoring system, said Alwin Bakkenes, head of global software engineering at Volvo Cars.

“Our brand Volvo is synonymous with safety, and safety is synonymous with trust,” Bakkenes said in an interview. “People get into our cars not expecting anything bad to happen, but they feel intrinsically that if they’re ever in a situation … we will do our utmost to keep people safe, to protect them from harm.”

Another important component is Volvo’s connected safety technology that allows its vehicles to exchange information about hazards and conditions ahead, including roadworks. Sharing this information can effectively extend the system’s awareness beyond what an individual vehicle’s sensors can detect, potentially improving the operating capabilities of the self-driving functionality.

Volvo plans to make the new point-to-point driving system available across its vehicle lineup, from entry-level to high-end versions — though the company didn’t reveal which models will come first. The timeline was also a little vague, with Bakkenes only confirming that it will launch “before the end of the decade.”

Kani also pointed to the commercial implications, noting that point-to-point driving may prove to be more valuable than a system limited to highway assistance. Nvidia sees the partnership as an opportunity not only to advance the technology but also to help Volvo develop its business model around ongoing software-based offerings, he said.

news.title: Memo: Accenture has told many employees, some of whom had been spending as much as $1,000 monthly, that it will now only spend $29 a month per person on Claude (Joseph Cox/404 Media)
news.title_en: Memo: Accenture has told many employees, some of whom had been spending as much as $1,000 monthly, that it will now only spend $29 a month per person on Claude (Joseph Cox/404 Media)
news.author: 404 Media
news.article_content:
The news is a snapshot of what continues to play out across all sorts of industries: companies have spent heavily on AI tools, and are now discovering that many users are burning or “chewing” through AI tokens at a rapid clip. In response, many companies have curbed their employees’ AI use. There is a special irony to Accenture doing much of the same, when it is a company that has encouraged its clients to invest heavily into AI.

“Claude Enterprise Users: Important Updates to Licensing and Usage Costs,” a recent internal Accenture announcement, seen by 404 Media, reads.

It says that effective October 1, Accenture introduced new changes to how Claude Enterprise costs are funded and charged. That includes centrally funding only $29 a month per person towards Claude usage.

Importantly, “all costs are consumption-based,” the announcement says. news.title: Anthropic says it is giving employee-like access to METR as part of its pledge to partner with evaluators for assessment of its models and safety practices (Anthropic)
news.title_en: Anthropic says it is giving employee-like access to METR as part of its pledge to partner with evaluators for assessment of its models and safety practices (Anthropic)
news.author: Anthropic
news.article_content:
ResearchPolicyCommitmentsLearnNewsTry ClaudeAnnouncementsAn update on independent evaluatorsOct 15, 2026Last month, we committed to stronger independent, third-party assessment of our models and safety practices. We also signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, in which companies pledged to partner with independent external auditors or evaluators. Today, we’re announcing that we’ve started to give employee-like access to a team from METR, a nonprofit that evaluates frontier AI models.

METR will publish the results of its risk assessments. Over the past year, we’ve worked with METR on several reviews of our Risk Reports. We’re also working with SecureBio and Accenture as evaluators, and are in early discussions with several other organizations, including Hugging Face.

As models have become more powerful, they’ve required stronger safeguards and more challenging risk assessments. We want to be publicly accountable for the decisions we’re making. But we can’t publicly share all the information relevant to our safety work. Some of it could be useful to malicious actors, or is commercially sensitive, like compute or training information. Instead, we’re giving third-party evaluators deep access to our information, and are having them share evidence and reasoned conclusions about the risks involved in building our models. We aim to close the gap between what evaluators understand about a frontier AI company’s systems and what the company itself understands.

Although the analogy isn’t exact, bank supervision operates on similar logic. Banks know more about their own risk positions than outsiders do, so regulators assign resident examiners to work inside the largest banks. If a bank’s risk-taking could threaten the public, third parties try to see that in advance.

For the AI industry, this is a step toward robust safety oversight. We’re moving quickly with multiple evaluators and learning actively about what kinds of partnership work. We’re committed to sharing updates as we go.

We’ve onboarded six METR employees with company hardware, office space, and access to internal tools and systems that are roughly on par with what our own risk assessment teams have access to. Outside a small number of clearly defined categories (e.g., data about customers, attorney-client privileged information, or information about our model architectures), Anthropic employees are encouraged to share information with them just as they would with a fellow employee working on alignment risk.1

METR will publish its analysis of our risk levels, incidents, or practices. Anthropic can’t veto publication, but we can require them to redact information if it falls into narrow, predefined categories like the ones above. METR is free to characterize our redactions publicly, and say whether it believes the redactions were justified, as long as it does so without revealing the redacted information.

Our engagement with METR is limited to a small team operating under enforceable agreements. Other METR employees are siloed from that team’s work, including researchers who work with us on other projects. Embedded evaluation gives a few qualified people working under Anthropic’s security standards a close view of how we operate. It’s not a way for other organizations to obtain our information, or that of our customers and partners.

We’re working on several other partnerships. Because these other partnerships are still in early stages, we’re providing these evaluators with more limited information, and they have more limited publication rights. Our goal with these early engagements is to make sure that our partners protect confidential information and have the requisite resources and expertise to evaluate our models. As partnerships progress and we build trust, we hope to fully embed more independent evaluators.

We’re developing three tiers of access for evaluators. Over time, we hope to have several evaluators at the third tier, with each team publishing their own analysis of our risk posture and key decisions.

In the first tier, evaluators conduct narrowly scoped risk investigations. We decide what access to provide a first-tier evaluator, and evaluators can publish their findings with our approval.

In the second tier, evaluators can publish without our approval, and they have access to more information. We can still require removal of specific categories of information, though evaluators can publish their views on whether our redactions were justified.

The third tier is the arrangement we’ve described with METR, with employee-like access and publication rights similar to those of the second tier.

SecureBio is currently in the first tier. It’s in the process of reviewing the chemical and biological weapons chapter of our August Risk Report, after completing and publishing a pilot review of our previous risk report. After this review is complete, we will consider moving to projects with increased access and publication rights.

With Accenture and Faculty, we're working toward an ambitious partnership that includes evaluating and red-teaming models, conducting alignment assessments, testing model safeguards, and building capabilities across our organizations.

We’re embedding evaluators voluntarily, and we believe every frontier AI company should do the same.

news.author: Axios

news.title: Meta says it worked with Apple to make Muse Spark Open run locally on M5 Ultra Mac Studios, letting users pair two to four Studios to code or do agentic work (CNBC)
news.title_en: Meta says it worked with Apple to make Muse Spark Open run locally on M5 Ultra Mac Studios, letting users pair two to four Studios to code or do agentic work (CNBC)
news.author: CNBC
news.article_content:
Tim Cook and Mark Zuckerberg have clashed for years, but with John Ternus taking the reins at Apple, the rivals are finding common ground in artificial intelligence.

Meta and Apple revealed a new collaboration Thursday that will enable developers to easily run Meta's new open-weight AI model on Apple's high-end desktop computers.

The collaboration centers on Muse Spark Open, the most capable open-weight model released under a license that allows for limited commercial use, according to Meta. It's an 816-billion-parameter model using a so-called mixture-of-experts architecture. As an open-weight model, developers can download the technology's parameters, or weights, from the internet and run the model on a wide range of hardware.

Customers will be able to pair between two and four Mac Studio PCs to use Muse Spark to code, analyze video or do other agentic work. The model runs locally, instead of in the cloud, adding a layer of security and saving users money, the companies said.

Thursday's announcement, following months of collaboration, is a sign that the AI boom has shifted historical alliances in Silicon Valley. For years, Apple and Meta regarded each other warily and avoided public partnerships, and the relationship hit rock bottom after Apple introduced privacy changes in 2021 that limited the targeting capabilities of digital ad companies. Meta estimated in early 2022 that the change would cut its revenue that year by $10 billion.

Representatives from Apple and Meta declined to say if the Muse Spark Open collaboration was the start of a deeper relationship.

Zuckerberg posted a picture on X showing the Meta agent working on a Mac computer. He wrote, "Muse Spark Open -- weights releasing today -- runs great on new Mac Studios thanks to work with @johnternus and Apple."

Ternus responded, "Congrats to the team! Amazing to run a model of Muse Spark Open's caliber and scale this efficiently, right from your desk. Mac Studio keeps pushing the boundaries of on-device AI!"

Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang said in an interview that many powerful open-weight models are too big to be run on the majority of personal computers, but Apple's Mac Studios make enough memory available to users so that it's practical to run Muse Spark Open.

The move represents an important show of confidence in Meta's rebooted AI efforts and could pose a challenge to OpenAI and Anthropic. It could also signal Apple's growing strength in AI chips, a market that Nvidia has dominated so far due to their prevalence in large data centers.

"We worked with Apple to bring leading Agent capabilities to your desktop for the first time on the Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios, so you know we're really excited about this," Wang said. Developers can download a version of the AI model from websites like Hugging Face without extra configuration for Apple's silicon. Muse Spark Open has also been tuned to run faster on Apple's hardware, and the iPhone maker revealed new benchmarks for its chips and published technical documentation about its MLX AI framework's ability to split open-source models across multiple machines.

Mac Studios aren't cheap though, and this AI model requires the fastest Apple chips and as much memory as possible.

Currently, a Mac Studio with the required M5 Ultra chip and 256GB of memory costs at least $10,799. A more expensive version with 512GB of RAM will be released later this month.

The two companies are collaborating on open-source AI, which has become a point of contention in Washington as politicians worry that free Chinese models could undercut American AI. Although Meta once centered its AI strategy on its older open-weight Llama family of models, it has since focused on creating proprietary models under the leadership of Wang, who joined Meta when the company invested more than $14 billion into his former startup Scale AI last year.

While Apple and Meta, then known as Facebook, partnered on iPhone extensions over a decade ago, they haven't struck any public partnerships since 2017 after Apple removed system-level Facebook integration from the iPhone.

"Most of the animosity predates my tenure at the company, but obviously there's been a long history between Meta and Apple," Wang said, pointing to one member of his team, AI researcher and former Apple director Daniel Gross, as a reason for the collaboration. Gross, along with former GitHub CEO Nat Friedman, was a major Zuckerberg hire last year as the Facebook founder was overhauling his company's AI strategy.

Cook, who was Apple CEO until Ternus succeeded him last month, took a shot at Zuckerberg in 2018, during the Cambridge Analytica scandal, saying, "I wouldn't be in this situation." Cook often criticized Meta for compromising user privacy.

Zuckerberg has also insulted Apple in public, telling Joe Rogan last year that the company "hasn't invented anything great since the iPhone." Zuckerberg has long sought to find a platform that Meta can own so it's not beholden to Apple.

Ternus, a hardware engineer, has already started changing things at Apple, including when it releases products.

And Meta's developers haven't been able to resist Apple's products. The company bought hundreds of Mac computers so its Superintelligence team could experiment with local AI and agents earlier this year.

Meta is just the latest AI model developer to team up with Apple.

In 2024, Apple announced a partnership with OpenAI to integrate ChatGPT into Siri, although the integration "dramatically underperformed" and didn't lead to OpenAI user growth, OpenAI said in a filing that's part of a legal dispute with Elon Musk's xAI. Apple sued OpenAI in July, alleging trade secret theft, a claim OpenAI denied.

Earlier this year, Apple announced a deal with Google, to use its Gemini models in Apple Intelligence as well as Google Cloud infrastructure.

Still, Apple's AI strategy has drawn criticism from investors and customers in part because its new version of Siri, released last month, isn't as advanced as chatbots and agents from leading labs.

Meanwhile, Meta has bet big on becoming a leading lab but has struggled to keep up with the competition and its business remains almost entirely reliant on ads. Recent developments, such as Meta's Muse personal agent app and its latest proprietary foundation model, Muse Wonder, released earlier this week, have begun to excite investors who are optimistic about new AI business opportunities.

Open source remains part of Zuckerberg's AI strategy. In August, Meta debuted a small open-weight AI model dubbed Muse Glimmer, with Zuckerberg pledging to eventually release something bigger and more powerful.

Muse Spark Open isn't as advanced as Muse Wonder, a proprietary offering, but Wang said it's good enough to potentially entice more coders to upgrade.

"These aren't the most capable models that we've developed or released," Wang said. "But we think that there will be a lot of companies and developers who sort of use this model and tinker with it at small scale and then seek to ramp up and scale up their usage."

WATCH: Apple makes its biggest smart-home push yet under CEO John Ternus.

news.title: Meta releases Muse Spark Open, saying it is the most capable US open-weight model, with 816B total and 42B active parameters and a 1M-token context window (Meta AI Research)
news.title_en: Meta releases Muse Spark Open, saying it is the most capable US open-weight model, with 816B total and 42B active parameters and a 1M-token context window (Meta AI Research)
news.author: Meta AI Research
news.article_content:
Today, we’re releasing the weights for Muse Spark Open, the most capable US open-weight model to date. Muse Spark Open is a natively multimodal model with 816B total parameters (42B active) and a 1M-token context window. Built for coding and agentic work, it excels at long-horizon tasks, complex software engineering, and multi-step reasoning.

We believe the future is for everyone, and that includes the freedom to run advanced models wherever, including at home. Muse Spark Open is the first model in its class to run on your desktop using two Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios with the latest MLX framework.

Muse Spark Open is available today through API platforms at Baseten, Fireworks AI, Groq, Modal, Nebius, OpenRouter and Together AI. Model weights are available for download on Amazon SageMaker AI, Google Cloud Model Garden, Hugging Face, and Microsoft Foundry Models.

It runs on leading inference engines like SGLang, vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, Hugging Face Transformers, Apple MLX, llama.cpp, and Unsloth with optimizations for AMD, Apple, Intel, and NVIDIA silicon. Developers can easily further customize the model using the PyTorch framework.

Key BenchmarksOptimized for Apple SiliconAvailable NowSafety and PreparednessLicenseGet StartedKey Benchmarks

For more details about our evaluations, see the evaluation methodology report.

Leveraging the latest version of MLX, Muse Spark Open was optimized to run on Mac Studio with M5 Ultra, and together they’re the best way to run a powerful model on your own desktop.

Apple’s unified memory architecture lets the M5 Ultra's integrated GPU use up to 512 GB per Mac Studio, so two machines can hold an entire model. And the chip’s 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth is fast enough to read the small slice each token needs. The result is two Mac Studios behave like one supercomputer with a terabyte of unified memory.

We tested a range of agentic workflows running entirely on-device, using Muse Code powered by Muse Spark Open, including shipping real iOS changes to Ice Cubes (an open-source Mastodon client) — bug fixes, new features, full build — and driving DaVinci Resolve end to end, with the model reviewing footage frame by frame to find the strongest moments and crop them vertically.

We’re sharing this work because we want everyone to have access to the best models. The open-weight version of Muse Spark ships with custom, auto-tunable Helion GPU kernels in SGLang, delivering 1.03-3.95× kernel-level speedups on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs, and a 3% end-to-end speedup on AMD MI350.

Releasing open-weight models is part of how we bring the benefits of personal superintelligence to everyone, and part of how safety work advances across the field.

Open weights also carry their own considerations, and Muse Spark Open has additional safety post-training for that reason. The results demonstrate strong safeguards across risk categories measured.

We evaluated the model in line with our Meta Superintelligence Scaling Framework, covering the most severe risks, and it met the thresholds our framework requires for release. Detailed results are in the Muse Spark Open model card, with a full evaluation report available soon.

We’re releasing the weights under the Muse Model License with limited commercial terms, which allow many developers to use the model for free.

You can customize Muse Spark Open for your use case by leveraging PyTorch’s TorchTitan to further tune the model. To run it on Apple silicon, use MLX, which pulls the weights directly from Hugging Face.

Muse Spark Open is available now through Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/collections/meta-models/muse-spark-open

Hosted Inference Partners: Together AI, Fireworks, Baseten, Modal, Groq, Nebius, and OpenRouter.

Built or published something with Muse Spark Open? Share with us on the Hugging Face Forums — we’d love to see what you create.

news.content_snippet: Binance.US is looking to raise as much as $100 million as the crypto exchange seeks to beef up its US business amid intensifying competition for digital-asset customers.
news.summary_en: Crypto exchange Binance.US is seeking to raise up to $100 million in a private round targeting a valuation of roughly $1 billion to fuel its American expansion. news.summary_en: Google has showcased Gemini 4 Argon, an embodied AI model designed to serve as a unified controller for robotics. The company’s existing Kaleido 3 displays can be found in e-readers and tablets from companies like Kobo, PocketBook, and Boox, while Amazon’s Kindle Colorsoft uses a customized version to improve performance. The new Kaleido 4 technology addresses some of Kaleido 3’s shortcomings with improved color reproduction, better contrast, and faster screen refreshes.

Other E Ink technologies, like its Gallery 3 display found in the Remarkable Paper Pro, use colored pigments that move around to form full-color images, but Kaleido 3 employs a color filter over an e-paper panel with just black and white pigments. That approach results in color e-paper screens with fast refresh rates, but it generates color images at a lower resolution with a limited palette that tends to make them look desaturated. The extra color filter also leaves plain text looking darker than it does on e-readers with only a black-and-white E Ink screen.

E Ink claims its new Kaleido 4 display tech doubles the “color gamut volume” of its predecessor, which should improve how color images look. However, the technology is still limited to producing just 4,096 colors (modern LCD and OLED displays can produce millions) and, as with Kaleido 3, at a lower resolution than black-and-white text is displayed. But Kaleido 4 does increase white reflectance by 15 percent and boosts contrast by 50 percent, so plain text will potentially look less muddy than it often does with Kaleido 3.

The reason that E Ink’s seemingly superior Gallery 3 technology hasn’t been used in more devices is because those displays have a slow refresh rate that can often feel frustrating to use. Kaleido 3 refreshes much faster, and thanks to a new oxide TFT backplane (that sounds similar to what the Kindle Colorsoft uses), Kaleido 4’s performance is even faster with refresh rates up to 18fps, making the screens capable of playing back video.

Companies like Amazon and Kobo haven’t yet announced any new devices that will feature Kaleido 4 screens, but Hanvon Technology will be the first to adopt the new technology in its upcoming M10C II tablet. It will only be available in China, but the M10C II will feature a Kaleido 4 display with a micro-etched tempered-glass surface designed to reduce glare while providing a more authentic paper-like feel when taking notes using its battery-free pen.

news.summary_en: E Ink has unveiled its next-generation Kaleido 4 color e-paper technology, premiering in an upcoming digital note-taking tablet in China. Engineered to succeed Kaleido 3—found in leading e-readers—the new display resolves long-standing issues by delivering richer color saturation, superior contrast, and snappier refresh rates. The upgrade reinforces E Ink's firm grip on the digital reading display supply chain.
news.title_zh: E Ink推出了下一代彩色电子纸技术Kaleido 4，取代了目前被亚马逊、Kobo和PocketBook等品牌使用的Kaleido 3显示屏。
news.summary_zh: 元太科技发布Kaleido 4彩色电子纸，全面提升对比度与色彩饱和表现

news.summary_en: As consumer AI assistants rapidly climb app store charts with millions of downloads, privacy advocates are ringing alarms over unchecked social data harvesting. Users are prompted to grant permissions that siphon entire contact lists and historical logs, effectively feeding the private details of friends and acquaintances into AI models without consent. This trend marks a shift toward passive, non-consensual surveillance disguised as helpful personalization.
news.title_zh: 朋友不会让朋友把自己的数据提供给人工智能代理
news.summary_zh: 消费级AI助理爆火背后暗藏侵权隐患，用户通讯录与亲友隐私未经授权遭批量摄取

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 随着Meta等科技巨头旗下的消费级个人AI助手登顶应用商店并积累数百万下载量，其背后的数据捕获机制引发了广泛的隐私伦理争议。为了构建个性化画像，这类智能体在安装时往往要求获取用户的全部社交通讯录与过往交互记录，导致用户亲友乃至普通泛关系链成员在毫无知情权与授权的前提下被喂入模型训练库。这种‘替他人交出数据’的商业模式，正引发监管界对无知情被动监控的高度警惕。

Users are prompted to grant permissions that siphon entire contact lists and historical logs, effectively feeding the private details of friends and acquaintances into AI models without consent. This trend marks a shift toward passive, non-consensual surveillance disguised as helpful personalization.

elements_zh.where: 移动端应用生态及隐私合规领域

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 当年社交网络用通讯录推荐好友，现在AI助理直接把你前任和远房亲戚的聊天黑历史打包进训练集。科技巨头的温情话术永远是‘为了让你更省心’，而事实是只要你有一个热衷尝鲜的赛博孝子朋友，你的隐私就已经在硅谷的数据中心里裸奔了。
ai_analysis.insight_en: Social apps used to just spam your contacts for friend suggestions; now AI agents are casually indexing your ex's birthday and private text logs to make their bot 'friendlier.' The unspoken reality of consumer AI is brutal: all it takes is one tech-enthusiast buddy hitting 'Allow Access' for your entire life to end up in a training pipeline.

news.author: VentureBeat
news.original_content:
Carl Franzen / VentureBeat:
Nvidia launches Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, a 120B-parameter open model for enterprise agents, and says it outperforms frontier models on specialized benchmarks  —  An enterprise agent reviewing a credit agreement may need to extract figures
news.content_snippet: An enterprise agent reviewing a credit agreement may need to extract figures from tables, interpret a chart, check a related webpage …
news.summary_en: Nvidia has launched Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, a 120-billion-parameter open visual-language model tailored for enterprise agents. Optimized to parse dense visual documents such as legal agreements and financial matrices, Nvidia claims it outperforms frontier models on specialized business benchmarks. The release reinforces the chipmaker's push to solidify its enterprise software and agentic stack.
news.title_zh: Nvidia 推出 Nemotron 3.5 Super VL，这是一种面向企业代理的 120B 参数开放模型，并表示它在专业基准测试中优于前沿模型
news.summary_zh: Nvidia 推出 Nemotron 3.5 Super VL，这是一种面向企业代理的 120B 参数开放模型，并表示它在专业基准测试中优于前沿模型。相关动态引发全球产业界广泛讨论与技术跟踪。

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 英伟达正式发布参数量达1200亿的开放模型Nemotron 3.5 Super VL，专为企业级智能体自动化任务与高精度视觉理解设计。该模型聚焦于复杂商业场景中的视觉信息解析，如复杂信贷协议、财务报表中的微小数据提取以及多图表跨页对照分析，并在多项专业企业基准中超越了现有前沿商用模型。英伟达意在通过提供开箱即用的工业级底座，进一步强化其在企业端全栈AI软件生态上的话语权。

elements_en.where: Enterprise AI software and compute ecosystem
elements_en.what: Released Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, a 120B-parameter vision-language model
elements_en.why: Deepening software moat across enterprise workflows to fuel continuous GPU consumption

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 皮衣刀客深谙卖水人的致富经：不仅要把铲子卖出天价，还要亲自设计一套矿井图纸。发布一个能看懂借贷合同的120B模型，表面上是帮打工人告别加班对账，背地里算盘珠子响彻云霄——跑这个庞然大物，你们机房又得加购几组服务器柜子了。
ai_analysis.insight_en: Jensen Huang is an absolute master of pick-and-shovel economics: don't just sell the hardware, design the mine shafts too. Rolling out a 120B parameter model to read PDF contracts looks like enterprise charity, until you realize the compute required to host it keeps server farms buying high-margin GPUs forever.

news.title: GPT-6-Astra solves 49 of 50 physics research problems at $2.40 apiece
news.title_en: GPT-6-Astra solves 49 of 50 physics research problems at $2.40 apiece
news.author: THE DECODER
news.article_content:
On the TheoPhysEval benchmark, GPT-6-Astra solves 49 of 50 unpublished theoretical physics calculations as accurately as leading specialists. In some cases where the agent seemed to fail, the experts' own reference solutions turned out to contain errors. But the researchers say physics hasn't had a breakthrough like the ones in mathematics, because the agents lack "taste." They still think autonomous, top-level AI research could arrive soon. They already see consequences for how young physicists are trained and for equal opportunity in the field.

news.author: The Verge AI
news.article_content: Microsoft and Nvidia held a launch party for the first wave of RTX Spark laptops last week in San Francisco, where a new wave of AI PCs took center stage amid a packed crowd and a lively hands-on area. The incident highlights the systemic failure of paid verification badges, which now actively facilitate the spread of malicious deepfakes instead of preventing fraud.

news.summary_zh: 带蓝V认证的仿冒账号发布女星米娅·高斯AI合成图获海量传播，平台认证机制形同虚设引发安全恐慌

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 拥有过百万粉丝且带有官方蓝V认证的高仿账号在社交平台上发布了女星米娅·高斯（Mia Goth）的AI合成肖像，借其离婚事件配以挑衅标语引发病毒式传播。该事件暴露出主流社交平台在付费蓝标机制普及后，身份审核系统彻底崩盘，使得深度伪造内容得以披着官方认证外衣大肆敛财并操纵舆论。

The incident highlights the systemic failure of paid verification badges, which now actively facilitate the spread of malicious deepfakes instead of preventing fraud.

elements_en.who: Verified imposter account and actress Mia Goth
elements_en.what: Circulated an AI-generated deepfake celebrity photo leveraging divorce gossip to go viral
elements_en.why: Platform pay-to-verify schemes lack genuine identity checks, enabling low-cost fraud

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 以前蓝V代表‘如假包换’，现在8美元一个月直接升级为‘官方认证诈骗’。生成式AI把造假门槛降到了地板，平台审核团队为了省成本却把眼睛全闭上了，最后受害的除了被造黄谣的名人，就是交了智商税的普通吃瓜群众。
ai_analysis.insight_en: Verification badges used to guarantee authenticity; now an $8 monthly subscription basically gets you an officially rubber-stamped deepfake syndicate. Generative AI flattened the cost of forgery, while platforms slashed trust-and-safety teams to pad margins.

news.title: Benn Jordan on Flock, privacy, and the new surveillance backlash
news.title_en: Benn Jordan on Flock, privacy, and the new surveillance backlash
news.author: The Verge AI
news.article_content:
Today, I’m talking with Benn Jordan, musician, YouTuber, researcher, and investigative journalist. You might know Benn from those first two titles — he’s got a prolific discography of experimental music dating back decades.

But in the last couple of years, he’s become a high-profile face in the creator and media spaces for his work investigating Flock Safety, the maker of automatic license plate readers and the software that powers them.

Benn recently testified in front of Congress, at a hearing the Senate Judiciary Committee’s Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism held, dedicated to Flock and other ALPR systems. This hearing felt like the culmination of months and months of growing criticism and bipartisan backlash against Flock — all of which is taking a shape similar to the pushback against AI data centers.

news.title_zh: 车牌识别监控遭国会严审，全美掀起反AI监控浪潮
news.summary_zh: 调查记者在美参议院听证会痛批车牌监控巨头Flock，AI大规模监控侵犯公民隐私引发两党强烈反弹

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 知名调查记者本·乔丹（Benn Jordan）在美参议院司法委员会听证会上，就智能车牌识别系统厂商Flock Safety对公众的大规模无差别监控发表严正证词。全美范围内因过度部署AI自动化车牌追踪与数据共享系统引发强烈隐私反弹，其遭遇的跨党派抵制浪潮正逐渐演变为对无节制AI监控基础设施的全面围剿。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Investigative journalist Benn Jordan testified before the Senate Judiciary Committee regarding widespread privacy violations by AI license-plate reader maker Flock Safety. The bipartisan pushback against rampant surveillance networks mirrors the growing societal resistance against unchecked AI data centers.

elements_en.what: Testified on the mass surveillance overreach of AI license-plate reader maker Flock Safety
elements_en.why: Rampant AI monitoring infrastructure is triggering severe bipartisan privacy concerns

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 大厂宣传里这是‘智能安防守护社区’，现实里这是‘全天候无死角记录你几点几分去了哪家汽车旅馆’。当AI摄像头连你车牌上的反光都能精准解析并卖给第三方时，所谓的安全感不过是把全套数字镣铐包装成了高科技礼物。
ai_analysis.insight_en: PR reps call it smart community safety; reality shows it is tracking down to the minute when you visited a cheap motel. When automated cameras monetize your movement under the guise of security, you haven't bought safety—you've bought a subscription to your own digital panopticon.

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 总部位于美国波特兰的服务器架构初创公司Mueon宣布完成6500万美元融资，由Maverick Silicon领投、芯片巨头英特尔跟投。该公司主打新型AI服务器机架系统，宣称其独特的硬件架构能在相同空间内提升最高10倍的计算密度，旨在解决当前大型数据中心在电力和物理空间逼近极限的瓶颈。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Portland-based hardware startup Mueon raised $65 million in a round led by Maverick Silicon, with participation from Intel. The company develops AI server rack architectures designed to pack up to 10x more computing capacity into standard footprint spaces, addressing data center density limits.

elements_zh.who: 硬件初创公司Mueon、领投方Maverick Silicon与英特尔
elements_zh.where: 美国波特兰及全球算力硬件市场
elements_zh.what: 完成6500万美元融资以研发算力密度提升10倍的新型服务器机架
elements_zh.why: 生成式大模型集群急剧推高空间与功耗成本，数据中心亟需物理层突破

elements_en.who: Hardware startup Mueon, Maverick Silicon, and Intel
elements_en.where: Portland, Oregon, and the global AI infrastructure market
elements_en.what: Raised $65 million to engineer server racks boasting up to 10x compute capacity
elements_en.why: Surging AI training demands have pushed datacenter power and floor space to physical limits

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 10倍密度提升听起来很科幻，散热工程师听了恐怕直接冷汗直流。在数据中心连变压器都不够用的今天，吹嘘算力密度的大多只负责画饼，最后往往发现限制你的不是芯片排布，而是隔壁发电厂能不能多烧两吨煤。
ai_analysis.insight_en: A 10x density boost sounds like sci-fi until the thermal engineers start having panic attacks. In an era where datacenters are already capped by local substations, cramming ten times more silicon together just means your thermal limits arrive ten times faster.

Claims up to 10x increase in compute density per rack
Targets urgent datacenter footprint and physical infrastructure constraints

news.content_snippet: North.cloud, which helps companies watch their cloud, AI and data spend, closed a $60 million Series B led by PeakSpan Capital, CEO Matt Biringer tells Axios Pro exclusively.
news.summary_en: North.cloud, a platform enabling enterprises to monitor cloud, AI, and data expenditures, raised a $60 million Series B round led by PeakSpan Capital, bringing total funding to $67 million. The startup helps businesses rein in runaway GPU and LLM operational expenses.
news.title_zh: 监控企业算力账单，云与AI支出管理平台获六千万美元B轮
news.summary_zh: 云成本管理平台North.cloud获6000万美元B轮融资，专注帮企业切断AI算力账单黑洞

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 专注监控云服务、AI调用及数据开销的初创平台North.cloud完成6000万美元B轮融资，由PeakSpan Capital领投，累计融资总额达6700万美元。该软件主要帮助企业实时追踪其基础设施与大模型API的隐性消耗，防止因团队无节制调用LLM和云端GPU而导致财务账单彻底失控。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: North.cloud, a platform enabling enterprises to monitor cloud, AI, and data expenditures, raised a $60 million Series B round led by PeakSpan Capital, bringing total funding to $67 million. The startup helps businesses rein in runaway GPU and LLM operational expenses.

elements_zh.where: 企业级SaaS及云成本优化市场

elements_en.where: Enterprise SaaS and cloud cost observability sector
elements_en.what: Closed a $60 million Series B round to expand cloud and AI spend monitoring
elements_en.why: Surging enterprise inference and GPU costs have made spending guardrails an urgent priority

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 淘金热里卖铲子赚了钱，现在连‘教淘金客怎么少买两把贵铲子’的咨询师都能融到几千万。企业过去一年疯狂堆AI模型，直到月底看到云厂商账单那一刻，才惊觉自己雇了一帮24小时不停烧钱吞Token的败家子。
ai_analysis.insight_en: In the AI gold rush, selling shovels made fortunes, and now selling a dashboard that tells you you bought too many shovels gets you $60M. CFOs spent all year screaming for AI adoption, only to panic at the month-end cloud invoice and realize their token bill is bankrupting them.

news.title: An interview with John Ternus, who says the memory shortage is "a crisis" and "all options should be on the table", and that Tim Cook "has great relationships" (Andrew R. Chow/Time)
news.title_en: An interview with John Ternus, who says the memory shortage is "a crisis" and "all options should be on the table", and that Tim Cook "has great relationships" (Andrew R. Chow/Time)
news.author: Time
news.article_content:
Andrew R. Chow/Cupertino, Calif.Follow this author to personalize your feed and get instant alerts.

Devin Oktar Yalkin for TIMEJust below the broad smile he’s been wearing all morning, John Ternus’ hands are shaking.

On this September day in Silicon Valley, Apple’s new CEO is surrounded by celebrities, tech enthusiasts, and reporters who have flocked to Apple Park from around the world to catch a glimpse of the company’s new and long-awaited foldable phone, the Duo. After Ternus takes a few photos with the device, an Apple PR rep pulls the influencer known as IShowSpeed out of the crowd to meet him. Winning over the 21-year-old isn’t exactly the toughest assignment Ternus has faced in his 25-year Apple career: Speed barks when he sees the phone and then gleefully springs into a backflip.

Ternus, who took over as CEO on Sept. 1, was chosen to run Apple because he has ably applied his engineering and design expertise to shape products that redefined entire categories of technology, from the Mac to iPad to AirPods and the iPhone. But becoming the face and front man for the second biggest company in the world by market cap is another proposition entirely. Ternus’ hard technical skills may not translate easily to a position that involves toggling from Hollywood to stockholders, to politicians shaping policy, to rival CEOs in the constellation of tech companies whose power challenges nation-states.

His predecessor, Tim Cook, gained stature on the world stage as a power broker deftly navigating global politics, markets, and supply chains. Cook’s predecessor, Steve Jobs, was a rock-star visionary who sold the world on the deeply personal and even spiritual nature of tech creations. Ternus is different from both: a private, detail-oriented engineer, little known outside the company until he became a senior hardware executive in 2021.

Rather than try to replicate his forerunners’ styles of success, Ternus has so far played to his own strengths—which are also those of Apple, a company that first and foremost builds beautiful products that spark productivity, creativity, and joy. Ternus’ interaction with IShowSpeed is clearly designed to capture this (and, of course, to goose preorder numbers among the influencer’s young and massive audience). To some critics, however, the scene might read as a legacy company aura-farming to sell expensive gizmos instead of building the actual technological future, which is artificial intelligence.

Virtually every one of Apple’s fellow Goliaths—Microsoft, Google, Meta, Amazon, and now Nvidia, OpenAI, and Anthropic—have flung themselves into the AI arms race, pouring hundreds of billions of dollars into training ever more intelligent thinking machines. While Apple trains its own models, it is nowhere near the technology’s frontier, leaving the company vulnerable to being left behind if super-smart AI transforms industry and society in the coming years. At the end of September, Apple was conspicuously absent when President Donald Trump hosted a luncheon for AI power players like SpaceX’s Elon Musk, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, and Google’s Sundar Pichai, who lobbied him on their visions for America’s tech future.

But Ternus and other Apple executives say they aren’t concerned. In the midst of a populist AI backlash, they contend that they are building a modest but personalized and privacy-preserving form of AI that will actually help ordinary people as opposed to merely dazzling Silicon Valley’s “lunatic fringe,” as Greg Joswiak, senior vice president of worldwide marketing, puts it. And besides, Ternus argues, even if other companies succeed in their mission of building super-intelligence, users will still want to talk to it on Apple devices.

“People want physical things,” he says a week later at the company’s flagship store on Fifth Avenue in New York City, wearing an amiable but guarded smile. He spent the morning greeting superfans who had lined up all night to get their hands on the iPhone 18. “They want to talk, to see images of loved ones, to take pictures. So I don’t see a scenario where all of a sudden, our devices disappear and we don’t have a need for an iPhone.”

Ternus is barely older than the company he’s running. Born in 1975 in Orange County—Apple was founded in ’76, just 400 miles north—he grew up as Steve Jobs was redefining the personal computer as a societal force. When Ternus was 8 years old, his father bought an Apple II. “I started playing games on it and fell in love with Apple,” he says. A decade later, he took his family’s newer Mac, an SE model, to college at the University of Pennsylvania, where he studied mechanical engineering.

In 2001, Ternus left a virtual reality company to join Apple at 26 as an engineer. He has now spent half his life at the company, rising through the ranks on his propensity to consider both how products are made and how the user will experience them. “John was really at the center of driving the spirit of collaboration across the company to make sure that end-to-end these products give you that delightful experience—and the technology kind of disappears as you’re using it,” says Richard Dinh, Apple’s vice president of product design.

Over the past 15 years, some critics have accused Apple of failing to innovate the way it did in previous eras, when the company popularized the home computer, the MP3 player, and the smartphone. But it is undeniable that Apple’s core products—its computers and phones—have remained elite thanks to behind-the-scenes innovations in hardware and software. And Ternus, Apple executives say, has been a big part of these improvements.

When Cook, 65, announced in April he would step down following a 15-year tenure, it was no surprise that the company tapped Ternus as his successor. Other executives describe him as pragmatic, meticulous, and unifying. “Ternus is a logical pick,” says Neil Cybart, an analyst who has been following Apple for more than a decade on his site Above Avalon. “He has been a big believer in this design-first culture that defines Apple, as well as the idea that it’s not just technology here; there needs to be something more.”

In the late 2010s, Apple executives shifted their messaging to focus more on fast-growing services like iCloud, the App Store, and Apple Music. But growth in service revenue has moderated this year, and the promotion of Ternus, a hardware and product guru, signals a return to the company’s roots.

So it’s fitting that his ascension coincided with the announcement of the Duo, Apple’s most radical design change to the iPhone since its 2007 release. Apple has been exploring the concept for years. In 2011, when many people still carried around flip phones, Ternus and five other engineers filed a patent application for foldable electronic devices, exploring what kind of batteries and circuit boards might be needed for such an idea. “It felt clear that we were going to eventually get to a place where OLED displays were going to be flexible,” Ternus says.

Many challenges stood in between the patent and the final product. The first attempts at a foldable smartphone in the 2010s from other companies tended to be fragile and not all that useful, with a big, ugly crease in the center interrupting the experience. “The other examples in the world felt kind of cheap and crappy,” Ternus says.

Across hardware and software teams, Apple engineers and designers got to work. With advancements in Apple silicon chips, they created a new display engine that facilitates seamless transitions between the inner and outer screens. They redesigned iOS to move the phone’s main controls from the bottom to the right side for easier thumb access.

Along the way, Ternus encouraged the team to invest more time and effort in the project, even as other foldables beat them to market. Dinh says that at one point, he asked Ternus whether his team should proceed with a top surface material similar to those of its competitors, which Dinh felt had flaws but was potentially good enough.

“And he was like, ‘Look, Rich, you’ll know when it’s the right thing.’ And that gave us the confidence to really push the boundaries on innovation and manufacturing, and fly worldwide to connect our suppliers together and come up with the nanotexture [a surface technology],” Dinh says. The result—a surface made from a custom polymer and built atop a hinge with more than 100 tiny interior precision components—has impressed its first users, who have said they can barely detect a crease at all.

Ultimately, the Duo promises a passport-size phone that opens into a powerful tablet. Users can stow it in their pockets, then open it up and watch a movie on its matte, light-deflecting surface. They can compare websites side by side, play touchscreen games with intricate detail, and use a dual-camera setup to simultaneously show themselves and what they’re seeing on FaceTime.

Of course, the Duo’s success is far from guaranteed. It could go the way of Apple flops like the Apple Car, which was never released, or the Vision Pro, which had staggeringly low sales in the last year. Certainly many prospective buyers will blanch at the device’s $2,000-plus price tag.

The opening motion of the hinge on Apple's newest invention, the iPhone Duo. HAW-LIN SERVICES

A look inside the iPhone Duo's internal structure. HAW-LIN SERVICES

But the phone’s first public testers have given glowing feedback. And demand for the Duo’s closest rival, Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold8, has been strong, suggesting there is a growing appetite for the foldables category, especially in Asia.

Apple also hopes that the Duo will earn a cultural cachet among storytellers and other artists, many of whom, like loyal Apple customers, still regard the company more as a maker of useful tools rather than as the enemy Big Tech has become. Four-time Oscar winner Sean Baker (Anora), who spoke at a “no-AI” film festival earlier this year, attended the Duo announcement in Cupertino and described his relationship with Apple as collaborative. “It’s not just ‘buy or use our product’—it’s much more of a working relationship where they stay in touch and ask us for feedback,” he says.

Baker noted that Apple’s products often underpin many parts of the filmmaking process. For instance, when moviemakers need to add dialogue in postproduction, they often simply record on an iPhone, because it’s convenient and nearly production-grade.

In person, Ternus presents as a guy trying to blend in: he dresses in nondescript clothes and speaks in platitudes, often about the brilliance of Apple’s internal culture. He has devoted much of his early tenure as CEO to obsessing over design, spending multiple days a week in the studio with the industrial-design and human-interface teams.

But beyond Apple Park’s gleaming, curved walls, Ternus has tough choices to make. Case in point: the ongoing global shortage of memory chips, which has raised costs and delayed production timelines. In July, the Financial Times reported that Apple had begun testing memory chips made by a Chinese company as a way to increase supply. That drew a swift rebuke from a bipartisan group of Senators, who wrote a letter to Apple arguing that to do so would imperil national security.

Ternus pushes back on that idea. “The constraints in memory are absolutely a crisis,” he tells TIME in the second of two interviews during September. “So our fundamental belief is that all options should be on the table.”

Cook was skilled at managing relationships with governments around the world, vigorously defending Apple’s interests even if it made him a target of ridicule. His courtship of Trump, which included a widely maligned presentation of a disc with a 24-karat gold base at the White House in 2025, helped Apple secure relief from some of the Administration’s most punishing proposed levies.

They can compare websites side by side, play touchscreen games with intricate detail, and use a dual-camera setup to simultaneously show themselves and what they’re seeing on FaceTime.

Of course, the Duo’s success is far from guaranteed. It could go the way of Apple flops like the Apple Car, which was never released, or the Vision Pro, which had staggeringly low sales in the last year. Certainly many prospective buyers will blanch at the device’s $2,000-plus price tag.

The opening motion of the hinge on Apple's newest invention, the iPhone Duo. HAW-LIN SERVICES

A look inside the iPhone Duo's internal structure. HAW-LIN SERVICES

But the phone’s first public testers have given glowing feedback. And demand for the Duo’s closest rival, Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold8, has been strong, suggesting there is a growing appetite for the foldables category, especially in Asia.

Apple also hopes that the Duo will earn a cultural cachet among storytellers and other artists, many of whom, like loyal Apple customers, still regard the company more as a maker of useful tools rather than as the enemy Big Tech has become. Four-time Oscar winner Sean Baker (Anora), who spoke at a “no-AI” film festival earlier this year, attended the Duo announcement in Cupertino and described his relationship with Apple as collaborative. “It’s not just ‘buy or use our product’—it’s much more of a working relationship where they stay in touch and ask us for feedback,” he says.

Baker noted that Apple’s products often underpin many parts of the filmmaking process. For instance, when moviemakers need to add dialogue in postproduction, they often simply record on an iPhone, because it’s convenient and nearly production-grade.

In person, Ternus presents as a guy trying to blend in: he dresses in nondescript clothes and speaks in platitudes, often about the brilliance of Apple’s internal culture. He has devoted much of his early tenure as CEO to obsessing over design, spending multiple days a week in the studio with the industrial-design and human-interface teams.

But beyond Apple Park’s gleaming, curved walls, Ternus has tough choices to make. Case in point: the ongoing global shortage of memory chips, which has raised costs and delayed production timelines. In July, the Financial Times reported that Apple had begun testing memory chips made by a Chinese company as a way to increase supply. That drew a swift rebuke from a bipartisan group of Senators, who wrote a letter to Apple arguing that to do so would imperil national security.

Ternus pushes back on that idea. “The constraints in memory are absolutely a crisis,” he tells TIME in the second of two interviews during September. “So our fundamental belief is that all options should be on the table.”

Cook was skilled at managing relationships with governments around the world, vigorously defending Apple’s interests even if it made him a target of ridicule. His courtship of Trump, which included a widely maligned presentation of a disc with a 24-karat gold base at the White House in 2025, helped Apple secure relief from some of the Administration’s most punishing proposed levies.

news.summary_en: OpenAI introduced updates to its 'Study Mode' and educational offerings, focusing on active, inquiry-based learning. Instead of instantly generating answers, the model adopts a Socratic prompting framework to guide students step-by-step through critical thinking.
